title: Reining dopamine in

html:
The preceding subsections have progressively expanded the dopaminergic mandate: from a scalar TD reward-prediction error to a distributed, multi-timescale, multi-domain portfolio of credit assignment channels. Taken at face value, this generalization threatens to make the dopaminergic system appear unconstrained–a universal prediction-error engine capable of updating arbitrary representations across arbitrary cortical state spaces. Here, it is argued that two structural features prevent this from being the case. First, corticostriatal and mesocortical dopaminergic innervation are not evenly distributed across the cortex; they are strategically concentrated in cortical areas that process policy-relevant variables, meaning the BG’s credit assignment machinery is anatomically prohibited from modifying much of the brain’s representations. Second, and more deeply, the inputs that supply the prediction baseline to VTA and SNc dopamine neurons are not drawn from neutral cortical state spaces—they are heavily weighted toward interoceptive and homeostatic channels, which ensures that the dopaminergic system, however broad its learning scope, remains anchored to the organism’s biological preference distribution.

The corticostriatal projection is often summarized as involving "all of cortex," and as a first approximation that is broadly correct: classical tract-tracing in primates and modern whole-brain mapping in mice both show that the striatum receives topographically organized input from a very wide range of cortical territories, with corticostriatal neurons arising predominantly from layer V (which is implicated in action prediction 1) and, to a lesser extent, deep layer III rather than being uniformly distributed across cortical laminae 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Importantly, however, this coverage is highly unequal and functionally structured, not homogeneous: orbitomedial prefrontal, anterior cingulate, amygdalar, and hippocampal inputs are concentrated in ventromedial and ventral striatal territories; associative territories of caudate receive strong projections from dorsolateral and other lateral prefrontal, posterior parietal, and higher-order temporal association cortex; and sensorimotor cortex projects most strongly to dorsolateral putaminal/putamen-like sectors, yielding the familiar limbic-to-associative-to-sensorimotor gradient across the striatum 4, 7, 8. Primary sensory cortex lies at the extreme end of this organization, but not in the sense of simply bypassing the basal ganglia: rather, sensory cortical input is concentrated in specialized caudal/posterior striatal territories—including the tail/posterior striatum in rodents and the visual caudate-tail system in primates—which receive convergent corticostriatal, thalamostriatal, and distinctive nigrostriatal input and are implicated in sensory salience, stable stimulus-value learning, and sensory-guided orienting or action selection 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. Thus, the strongest version of the claim is not that early perceptual representations are excluded from basal-ganglia learning, but that basal-ganglia credit assignment is anatomically biased toward striatal territories that already integrate sensory, motivational, cognitive, and action-related information, while more direct sensory learning is funneled through specialized posterior channels rather than distributed uniformly across the canonical ventral-to-dorsolateral corticostriatal axis 4, 5, 9. Cortical input to the striatum is mapped in detail. (Figure). The corticostriatal loop is a re-entrant circuit. (Figure). Visual cortex sends direct projections to the striatum. (Figure). The visual corticostriatal loop runs through the caudate. (Figure).

The mesocortical dopaminergic projection appears to impose a complementary bias on the cortical side of the learning loop. In primates, dopaminergic innervation and dopaminoceptive machinery are not distributed uniformly across cortex: frontal association, cingulate, orbitomedial prefrontal, paralimbic, and at least some motor cortical territories receive especially prominent dopamine input, whereas many primary sensory areas tend to show sparser innervation, though not a complete absence of dopaminergic signaling 14, 15, 16, 17. This gradient should not be overstated into a sensory-versus-nonsensory dichotomy: dopamine receptors are present across cortical regions, including primary sensory cortex, but their regional densities and laminar patterns are heterogeneous, and cortical DARPP-32 expression is correspondingly selective rather than ubiquitous 18, 19. Within frontal cortex, D1 receptor signaling has been especially implicated in sculpting persistent delay-period activity and working-memory representations, with the characteristic inverted-U profile indicating that mesocortical dopamine is tuned to stabilize task-relevant representations rather than indiscriminately amplify cortical activity 20, 21. Taken together with the unequal corticostriatal projection pattern, the picture is not that the basal ganglia implements a universal learning rule over all cortical content, but that dopamine-dependent credit assignment is anatomically biased toward cortical state spaces that already participate in valuation, working memory, action selection, cognitive control, and policy expression, while exerting weaker and more specialized influence over early sensory representations 4, 6, 16.

The deeper constraint on dopaminergic error signaling is not whether dopamine can, in principle, report prediction errors over rich and abstract state spaces, but how the baseline and gain of those signals are conditioned by internal-state circuitry. On this point, the evidence supports a strong homeostatic influence without implying that VTA or SNc dopamine neurons are driven by a purely interoceptive channel: monosynaptic tracing shows that midbrain dopamine neurons integrate inputs from a highly heterogeneous afferent network, but hypothalamic and other autonomic/interoceptive regions are prominent components of that ensemble, and cell-type-specific mapping likewise identifies the lateral hypothalamus as one of the dominant long-range inputs to VTA dopamine neurons 22, 23. The lateral hypothalamus is especially important at this interface because LH->VTA circuitry carries information relevant to arousal, feeding, and motivational state through multiple molecularly distinct channels: GABAergic LH inputs can disinhibit dopamine neurons and increase nucleus-accumbens dopamine release, while orexin/hypocretin-, neurotensin-, and melanin-concentrating-hormone-related LH systems also modulate VTA function and reward-related behavior 24, 25, 26, 27. Arcuate hunger circuitry provides a more direct example of homeostatic state gating dopaminchatergic teaching signals across timescales: metabolic sensing in AgRP neurons is required for normal fasting-dependent increases in motivated sucrose seeking and for normal dopamine dynamics in both nucleus accumbens and dorsal striatum, supporting the view that AgRP neurons regulate the magnitude and temporal profile of striatal dopamine responses as a function of energy state rather than merely shifting tonic baseline activity 28. Conversely, melanocortin signaling supplies a satiety-linked constraint, but in a circuit-specific way that should not be collapsed into a single "POMC suppresses dopamine" rule: arcuate POMC neurons project to VTA dopamine neurons and can enhance sucrose motivation via MC3R signaling within the VTA, whereas α\alpha-MSH acting at MC4R in nucleus accumbens decreases sucrose motivation 29, 30. Thus, even if dopamine is generalized beyond a narrow scalar reward-prediction error, the circuitry that sets its operating point remains strongly tethered to homeostatic state: internal needs do not define the entire dopaminergic error code, but they do help set which prediction errors are amplified, when, and for what behavioral purpose.

The influence of homeostatic state on dopaminergic signaling extends beyond caloric balance to fluid and electrolyte regulation. In rats, thirst potentiates phasic VTA and nucleus-accumbens dopamine responses to water-predictive cues, and this effect can be mimicked in euvolemic animals by central angiotensin II, supporting the view that early dehydration signals can selectively amplify mesolimbic teaching signals for balance-restoring outcomes 31. More generally, this fits a broader principle already established for feeding: hunger augments phasic dopamine responses to food-predictive cues, and the hunger signal ghrelin can enhance cue-evoked mesolimbic dopamine, indicating that internal need states gate dopaminergic responses to predictive stimuli in a domain-specific manner rather than simply shifting a global reward baseline 31, 32. The relevant thirst circuitry begins in classic homeostatic structures of the lamina terminalis, especially the subfornical organ, whose neurons detect circulating and osmotic signals and can recruit downstream motivational circuitry to modulate dopamine responses; however, the exact relay from these first-order thirst sensors to VTA dopamine neurons is better described as an emerging circuit motif than as a single fully resolved linear pathway 31, 33. Sodium-appetite circuitry provides a parallel, though less fully characterized, route by which electrolyte state may reach midbrain reward systems: aldosterone-sensitive HSD2 neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract are key nodes in sodium-appetite control and send minor direct projections to the VTA, making a VTA interface anatomically plausible even if its functional contribution remains less firmly established than the thirst-related SFO pathway 34, 33. Taken together, the strongest claim is not that dopamine is reducible to a single homeostatic signal, but that midbrain dopamine neurons are embedded in a broader interoceptive network carrying information about hunger, hydration, and electrolyte need, such that internal state helps determine which cues and outcomes receive amplified dopaminergic credit assignment at a given moment 35, 36.

The most defensible computational reading of this architecture is that internal physiological state acts as a context-dependent modifier of outcome value and of the gain placed on dopaminergic teaching signals. In formal terms, this is closely aligned with a state-dependent reward function: in homeostatic reinforcement learning, an outcome is rewarding to the extent that the organism predicts it will reduce the deviation between current internal state and an ideal set point, and recent reviews of dopamine and interoception likewise argue that physiological need acts as an occasion setter or gain-control variable for phasic dopamine responses to cues and outcomes 37, 38. Consistent with that view, primary food and fluid rewards are rewarding in part because they correct homeostatic imbalance, and emerging accounts increasingly argue that at least the most basic forms of reinforcement should be understood as depending on interoceptive evaluations of an action’s effect on vital physiological variables rather than on sensory pleasure alone 39, 40, 36. The stronger claim—that general-purpose dopaminergic credit assignment is an evolutionary elaboration of an older homeostatic regulatory architecture—is therefore best presented as a principled hypothesis rather than as settled fact. It is well motivated by current theory and by the anatomy reviewed above, but the available evidence supports most directly the narrower conclusion that generalized prediction-error signaling in dopamine remains strongly constrained by internal-state and interoceptive control systems 40, 38.

A remaining (open) question is how the dopaminergic system acquires its homeostatic calibration. One compelling answer is developmental: in the neonatal period, the only contexts reliably driving strong positive dopaminergic prediction errors are those that correct acute homeostatic imbalances. In altricial mammals, virtually all early reward structure derives from maternal interaction—milk delivery corrects caloric and fluid depletion, thermal contact resolves cold stress, tactile stimulation regulates the autonomic and hormonal milieu. Because these are the events most reliably available in early postnatal life, and because they are intrinsically coupled to interoceptive repletion signals (gastric stretch, rising blood glucose, skin warming, declining cortisol), the first value functions the corticostriatal system learns are necessarily tethered to homeostatic set points. The predictions that VTA GABA neurons and LH projections encode as the infant’s first conditional expectations are predictions about interoceptive state, not abstract symbolic variables. This process can be understood as a developmental bootstrapping of the preference distribution: the hard-wired hypothalamic-VTA architecture (which ensures homeostatic signals can reach dopamine neurons) provides the structural substrate, while the earliest rounds of corticostriatal learning lock in the value of homeostatic correction as the implicit reference against which subsequent prediction errors are computed. Later-developing secondary rewards—social approval, monetary gain, aesthetic pleasure—acquire their dopaminergic significance through chains of associative and identity prediction errors anchored, ultimately, to that early-established homeostatic baseline. The implication for the computational architecture of the BG is that its "objective function" is not arbitrary: it is inherited from the survival-critical error signals that first activated the system’s teaching machinery, and this origin is preserved in the structural connectivity between hypothalamic homeostatic controllers and the midbrain dopaminergic nuclei that distribute the credit assignment signal.

The combined picture that emerges from these two constraints—selective corticostriatal and mesocortical access, and homeostatic grounding of the prediction baseline—is of a credit assignment system that is genuinely capable of generalized learning across a rich state space, but is not free to learn anything. The dopaminergic architecture is, in the relevant engineering sense, a constrained optimizer: its search space is restricted to policy-relevant cortical representations by anatomical connectivity, and its objective function is anchored to biological viability by the interoceptive weighting of its prediction baseline. The generalized prediction-error view of dopamine, far from implying an unconstrained learner, is best interpreted as describing a flexible optimization method operating within hard boundaries set by evolution, development, and anatomy—boundaries whose collective effect is to ensure that however much the dopaminergic system learns about sensory identity, associative structure, and action priors, it remains a tool for keeping the organism within its preference distribution. Striatal dopamine can enhance both fast working memory, and slow reinforcement learning, while reducing implicit effort cost sensitivity (Figure).
